Help page dat.cohen1981, examples: escalc(measure='ZCOR', ri=ri, ni=ni); rma(yi, vi), a random-effects model with one effect per row and no study level, so published_model is no. 20 correlations of course instructor ratings with student achievement; study labels repeat (16 studies, Centra 1977 and others give one correlation per course type, sample), so study is the grouping factor by the ruling on repeated clusters, inferred from the column, hence low. The rma heterogeneity term has no column (no row id). The source weights each effect by its sampling variance 1/(ni - 3), which the formula leaves out. Cohen (1981), via Cooper & Hedges (1994), Appendix A. Hand check #162: stands; 2 of the 16 study labels repeat.

formula: ri ~ 0 + interaction(var1, var2) + (0 + interaction(var1, var2) | study)
notes: The random term is an unstructured effect per correlation (the var1.var2 pair) within study, which random_slopes cannot name since the pair is no single covariate; the formula carries it and random_slopes stays blank, hence medium. Help page dat.craft2003, examples: tmp <- rcalc(ri ~ var1 + var2 | study, ni=ni) builds the var1.var2 pair and the sampling covariance V of the raw correlations; rma.mv(yi, V, mods = ~ 0 + var1.var2, random = ~ var1.var2 | study, struct='UN'). Multivariate meta-analysis of the 6 correlations among CSAI-2 cognitive anxiety (acog), somatic anxiety (asom), self-confidence (conf) and sport performance (perf) in 10 studies (studies 6 and 17 give a subset). The source weights the effects by V (from ni), which the formula leaves out. Craft et al. (2003), via Becker & Aloe (2019). Hand check #162: a structured covariance is named in the formula, so random_slopes stays blank against the outside check's interaction(var1, var2)|study, which names no covariate.

formula: cbind(events, total - events) ~ 0 + factor(dose) + (0 + factor(dose) | study), non-decreasing dose means, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck covariance over dose
documented_prior: mu_1 ~ Normal(mu*, sigma*), dose increments by a Gamma process of slope a and coefficient of variation c (mu* = -2, sigma* = 5, a = 0.667, c = 0.5 if the empirical MTD lies at most two increments above the first dose, else mu* = -4, sigma* = 3.5, a = 0.642, c = 0.5); sigma_m half-normal; OU length scale inverse-Gamma(1, 1)
notes: Hand check #162: Ursino, Roever, Zohar and Friede (2021, Ann Appl Stat 15:174-193; arxiv.org/abs/1908.06733), section 5.2, fit their Bayesian dose-finding meta-analysis (eqs. 1-3) to 10 of these 12 phase I studies of irinotecan and S-1 (Table 2; Yamada 2003 and Yoshioka 2009 not among them, the others equal cell for cell): events of total binomial, the logit toxicity a non-decreasing sum of dose increments plus study effects per dose that follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process over dose, the increments measured in 10 mg/m2. It replaces the reader's log-dose GLMM, written after Roever et al. (2022, Stat Med 41:3915-3940), who fit penalized logistic regressions per study and meta-analyze their estimates, no mixed model on this table. The help page only plots the curves. dose is a factor of 10 levels from 40 to 150 mg/m2; year is unused.

formula: cbind(deaths, n - deaths) ~ factor(study) + group + (0 + I(as.numeric(group == "Rosiglitazone")) | study)
notes: Help page example: pairwise(treat = group, event = deaths, n = n, studlab = study, sm = 'OR'), then metabin with method = 'glmm', model = 'CM.AL', random = TRUE, a random-effects conditional logistic GLMM (metafor's rma.glmm with the approximate hypergeometric likelihood), beside IV, Mantel-Haenszel, Peto and penalized logistic fits (Tian et al. 2009, Biostatistics). Conditioning on each trial's total events stands for fixed study effects, with a random treatment effect per study: written as factor(study) + group and a random rosiglitazone indicator by study, filed as an uncorrelated slope of group. 48 two-arm trials of rosiglitazone vs control; the six double-zero trials it adds are what separates it from dat.nissen2007. infarcts is the other outcome (Nissen and Wolski's primary), not modelled on the page; n.all counts all patients, n those with outcome data. intervention and detailed.intervention name the arm's drugs. Hand check #162: the slope sits on a 0/1 indicator, since (0 + group | study) gives each arm a random effect of its own (woods2010's form). CM.AL conditions the study intercepts of this model out on each trial's total deaths instead of estimating them, a binomial approximation with the offset log(n1/n2), so the model stands as published against the outside check.

formula: cbind(events, total - events) ~ 0 + factor(dose) + (0 + factor(dose) | study), non-decreasing dose means, Ornstein-Uhlenbeck covariance over dose
documented_prior: mu_1 ~ Normal(mu*, sigma*), dose increments by a Gamma process of slope a and coefficient of variation c (mu* = -2, sigma* = 5, a = 0.667, c = 0.5 if the empirical MTD lies at most two increments above the first dose, else mu* = -4, sigma* = 3.5, a = 0.642, c = 0.5); sigma_m half-normal; OU length scale inverse-Gamma(1, 1)
notes: Help page only plots the dose-toxicity curves per study (13 phase I trials of sorafenib, several doses each). The cited source Ursino, Roever, Zohar and Friede (2021, Ann Appl Stat 15:174-193; abstract read) fits a Bayesian curve-free hierarchical model on the logistic scale to these trials: a toxicity probability per dose with study random effects that follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck Gaussian process over doses, priors from a latent Gamma process. Roever et al. (2022) fit a two-stage penalized logistic regression and random-effects meta-analysis to both datasets (see dat.roever2022). Hand check #162: the paper (eqs. 1-3, section 5.1) fits these 13 trials and Jia et al. (2013), which the table lacks: events of total binomial, the logit toxicity a non-decreasing sum of dose increments plus study effects per dose that follow an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process over dose. A structured covariance is named in the formula, so the row stays published against the outside check's simplified intercept; the reader's shared study intercept is replaced.
